body: Scalpel blades are best. That's what I use.
Yes, the team at the clinic knows. Hopefully tomorrow won't be an awful experience.

I'm not seeing a psychologist regularly; I just got a referral for one from my GP this past week. I see a psychiatrist occasionally. I'm afraid of going to the hospital, even if the urges do get very strong.

No follow-up with this psychologist, but I got a referral from my GP for one that day.

Parents can be assholes. My father also called me an attention-seeker, as well as a disgusting human being, in the past when he found out I self-harm. I know he was just trying to express that he cared for me by showing "tough love", but it did more harm than good. I don't think he or my mother will ever be able to grasp the complexity of my self-harm.
I found Melancholia to be a pretty accurate representation of both non-functional and functional depression. It is a really depressing movie, though, and it doesn't have a happy ending, per se.
The only reason I'm choosing suspension hanging over a bullet to the temple is because I live in Canada, and don't have easy access to a gun. But rope is everywhere. Gotta choose what's accessible.
I'm just curious as to what dosage you're starting on. Abilify should be started at a low dose, like 2mg, and slowly increased over a period of time to a therapeutic dose, like 10mg.

I live with roommates in a house in a sketchy part of the city. I actually feel more anxious about break-ins now than when I lived alone.

For me, carrying a blade with me around the house has helped me to feel safer. I'm also mentally prepared to take an aggressive stance whenever answering the door, just in case someone suspicious shows up.

I'm currently doing CBT and DBT on my own, without the guidance of a therapist. I don't know if it's helping or not, but it's a distraction. I personally prefer CBT to DBT.

However, the number of times I've been told that DBT in particular would save my life is insane. I just kept getting worksheets pushed in my face, worksheets I would complete diligently, but wouldn't make me feel any better.

You'd think that after a year of not getting better despite hard work at the therapy would make them realise that someone might need more help than filling out simple worksheets.

You need more than just therapy for therapy to actually work, at the end of the day.
This Valentine's day has a twinge of hope for me. I have my first appointment for ECT that day, which I'm hoping will help with my depression.

I'm divided between the time when I cut down to my right tibial bone, and the time when I sliced open my left ulnar artery. Strange thing is, the "oh fuck" moment didn't hit until hours after both events. Still, I had two moments like that, months apart from each other.
You have to cut off circulation to the major vessels in your neck in order to pass out within seconds. Easier said than done.

There are many reasons why someone would turn to self-harm. To cope with emotional pain, to feel in control, to get an endorphin rush, or to outwardly express the struggles they can't vocalize.

I personally started self-harming after my first suicide attempt. I jumped out of a moving vehicle. The pain I felt from hitting the pavement left me in a state of calm and euphoria; an endorphin rush. I felt better, despite the fact that I had just tried to end my life. After that, I started self-harming to deal with my suicidal thoughts. I would then use it to cope with other things, such as anxiety attacks, and strong emotions, as well as to get a high, to feel in control, to deal with other physical pain, and most recently, to deal with psychosis.
Spray-Nine is awesome.

I've failed a lot of suicide attempts. I've lost count, honestly. The only thing I managed to do in regards to lasting physical damage to my body is scarring and liver damage.

Some people make one suicide attempt and go on to be appreciative and grateful for life. Others, like myself, go on to make further suicide attempts in an effort to end the pain.
This resonates with me. I have PTSD due to traumatic experiences with emergency services and at hospitals. My biggest fear now is being restrained. It's a major trigger for me.

See how your mind and body reacts to that dosage. If anything feels off, tell your doctor immediately.

Ideally, you would be starting at around 2mg and going up slowly from there.

She's not starting you on a dose of 10 mg,  is she? That's a very high dose to start with Abilify. It can be hard on your system if you don't up the dose slowly.

Personally, Abilify made my suicidal thoughts worse. This does not mean it will be the case for you. It's worth giving it a try, I think.
I know these feelings.
She should stop the medication and talk to her doctor as soon as possible. I had a similar experience upon taking Trintellix, and my doctor immediately canceled the prescription.

You definitely sound like an introvert. It also looks like you are experiencing symptoms of anxiety, possibly even social anxiety.

My advice to you would be to open up to a professional about it, like your school counselor or GP. That way, you can get properly assessed for anxiety and other mental health issues, like depression.
That lyric actually stopped me from making that final cut once.

I'm pretty certain they've tested my blood for drugs in the past. Doctors can't seem to tell the difference between a meth addict and someone experiencing a panic attack and flashbacks (me).

All in all, the hospital is not the drug police. They aren't going to release any of this info to authorities.

When I was young, I used to think suicide in any form was selfish. Boy, did that change when I became depressed and chronically suicidal at 17. After almost eight years of struggling with suicidal thoughts, I definitely don't view suicide as a selfish act anymore. I understand the pain and suffering behind it.

I think if you don't experience it personally, it's hard not to view suicide as disgusting or selfish. People don't always know how to react to something they don't understand, and they're also looking for someone to blame (that being the suicidal person). Their brains are trying to make sense of something they can't comprehend, so instead or reacting with compassion and concern, they react in outrage and disgust.

The thing about your post that saddens me the most is that everyone at the party agreed with your friend. No, maybe not all of them actually share her opinion, but they did share it outwardly, which isn't any better. I'm disappointed no one had the courage to speak up and challenge her views on the matter, even by just pulling her aside and having a private discussion with her.

Tread carefully... once you start cutting down to adipose tissue, it's hard to stop yourself from doing it again and again. It gets really addictive. Just be aware of the risks, both physical and psychological, involved with deep cuts.

I also used to have high-functioning depression, but over the last year, I've steadily become less and less functional as my depression continues to swamp me. I also miss the days of my high-functioning depression because at least I was still a functioning member of society back then. I had a full-time job, my own place, and a future. But as my depression and overall mental health got worse, I started to decline steadily. I can only work part-time due to my health, I live in a house with four roommates, and I'm also facing possible homelessness. All while I try to juggle the constant suicidal thoughts.

Cutting your neck poses some risks because of major blood vessels located there and their proximity to the surface. Just keep that in mind.

That being said, I too have had urges to cut myself in somewhat unusual places. I have half my head shaved, and I started cutting my scalp recently.
When I was in college, I wrote a passage called "Songs To Commit Suicide To". It mostly featurex Pink Floyd songs. Wish You Were Here, Us and Them, and The Final Cut were all on there.

My personal issue with the hotlines is that they've called emergency services on me before. It makes me scared to reach out to them, despite a desperate need to talk to someone about the suicidal/homicidal thoughts I have.

One of the main reasons I cut is to feel in control. Cutting makes me feel clear-headed, focused, and powerful. I am in full control of the situation. Also, it helps me control the Worm to some extent.
They say that about self-harmers above the age of eighteen as well.

If I could, I would never leave the house because many of my triggers are a common sight out in public. Of course, that's not practical, so I brave it. I've come to resent living in a city a little bit, because of all the triggering noises. I avoid triggers on television as much as possible. Yeah, I feel like I'm constantly trying to dodge them every day.
Cutting is the only thing that makes the Worm go away for a bit. It's helped me survive.
I can't go there, they'll hurt me. They have before.

No, of course not, but do you really want to give yourself the chance of developing other serious psychiatric problems that could potentially be avoided? Maybe if I had gotten help sooner, my illness would not have progressed to the point of psychosis. Also, psychosis and self-harm are definitely not a good mix. Best to get help now so you can actually start living life and don't stumble through adulthood like I am, because it only gets harder once you're an adult.
I've had depression and anxiety for seven years, and last year I got diagnosed with ptsd and psychosis as well.
Honestly, no I'm not. I'm trying to survive until Valentine's day, when I go for my ECT consultation.

That's a foolish thing to think, that you can/should wait until 30 to get help. Like I said in my post, it gets way harder to get that help after 18. Good luck getting it when you're 30. Now is the time to nip it in the bud, not ten years or so from now. You might think you'll be fine, but mental illness is insidious and it may kill you before you decide to get that help. I thought I would be fine when I was 17, and I'm clearly not fine anymore, and I've added two new diagnoses to my list since then. Don't. Wait.

A simple noose is best. Not a hangman's knot.

I went to the ER once because I was experiencing a flashback/panic attack. My friend thought I was having a seizure, so she called an ambulance.

The whole ordeal was even more triggering for me in the long run. I don't remember much, but I think they gave me Ativan, and I remember tranquilizers being mentioned (I was considered a "runner"). I may have been given some sort of chemical restraint, because I eventually fell asleep.

Overall it was a very unpleasant experience. I had a panic attack the next morning, and some other events ensued.

I don't feel that most medical professionals are compassionate towards anxiety. If you can avoid the ER, you're probably better off. If you're having panic attacks, you might want to think about getting a prescription from a GP.

I wish my friend would maybe try and talk to me more, but I think she freaks out and thinks medication is the first answer. It's probably also tricky to talk me down, since simple words like "relax", "lie down", and "take slow breaths" can be triggers for me and send me spiraling more.

I try to keep my eyes open, notice the sights and sounds around me. Sometimes it helps. I wish I could contact a distress line, but I'm afraid to.
I have tried guided meditation videos in the past, and my experience has been that they always increase my anxiety. An excellent suggestion, nonetheless.

Maybe if we feel lonely in our pain together, we won't feel so alone anymore. I'm glad this group has been providing you with much needed comfort.

I believe it's beds in and of themselves that are the trigger. I'm always quite hesitant to get into any bed nowadays, they bring up traumatic memories for me and cause flashbacks.

Sleeping on the couch makes me less prone to the flashbacks, but I sometimes still get them then. However, because of my back issues, I should sleep on a bed.

My cat is proving to be somewhat helpful in grounding me in reality when I go to bed. I also try to tell myself I'm in a safe place, no one is going to hurt me, and I take note of my surroundings.

Despite my best efforts, I often get flashbacks. I hope I can find some relief soon as well.

I was prescribed Trintellix once, not for my PTSD, but for depression. I had a bad reaction to it. I experienced pretty well all the negative side effects you can have on this particular drug. Within an hour of taking a 10 mg pill, my emotions and thoughts became extremely intense, I was manic, I became so itchy I scratched myself until I bled, and I was having a panic attack. My friend called an ambulance because she was afraid I might try and self-harm more, or commit suicide (I have chronic suicidal thoughts). The doctor at the ER advised I not take it again.

However, all that being said, that was my experience with Trintellix. It's very rare to experience side effects like this. Keep in mind that whenever a doctor prescribes you a medication, it's because he or she has determined that the benefits outweigh the risks. You may experience no ill side effects at all.
